agent_notes: The packet's KJV numbering (25:0, 25:1) shows that the KJV treats 'A Psalm of David' as a separate superscription verse. In the Hebrew the 'of David' is the first word of verse 1 and belongs to it, so I translate the whole verse as one. The lamed-prefix on David is ambiguous (by, of, for, belonging to David); I kept 'Of David' in the literal layer and did not choose authorship for the reader.

Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri differ on 'lift up my soul': prayer gesture (Lam 3:41), offering (Gen 43:34), or longing like a day-labourer (Deut 24:15). I did not pick one, and the dramatic layer keeps the image of lifting. The Radak/Meiri midrash on entrusting the spirit overnight is cited only as a reading they report, not as the meaning of the Hebrew.

agent_notes: KJV, ASV, Webster read the perfect with waw (וְסָלַחְתָּ) as a request 'pardon'. YLT keeps the plain perfect, 'Thou hast pardoned'. The form is a weqatal in a prayer where it carries the force of a request; the literal layer says 'and you will forgive' and the dramatic layer says 'forgive'.

The Hebrew 'rav hu' is 'great is it', and the 'it' is my 'iniquity' in the singular. I follow Meiri/Radak's point that the singular may be a specific wrong, but I do not name Bathsheba; the text does not.

Subject of יִבְחָר is disputed. Rashi, Radak and Meiri read God as the subject (the way God chooses for the man to walk); Metzudat David and Ibn Ezra (as Radak reports him) read the man (the way he chooses). The literal layer keeps the Hebrew ambiguous ('the way he chooses'); the dramatic layer follows the God-subject reading, as the older commentators do, and the commentary says so.

Literal layer: 'have made wide', with 'themselves' left to the reader, to hold both.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses קֹוֶיךָ as '[those who] wait for you'. I kept it and added 'hope' in the note because the same root קוה appears in v5 and v21 and carries both waiting and hoping. The commentary about Rashi on 'reikam' is cited from the packet; the cross-reference to Ps 7:5 is Rashi's own.

Hebrew בַאֲמִתֶּךָ is 'in your truth'. KJV, ASV and Webster say 'in thy truth'; BBE says 'in the true way'. I keep 'truth' and explain 'emet' as reliability in the note rather than choosing 'faithfulness' in the literal layer.
STEPBible glosses אוֹתְךָ as '<obj.> you'. I glossed it [obj] you as the skill asks. YLT's 'Near Thee' is a mistake for the object marker, not a reading.

STEPBible glosses מֵעוֹלָם as 'from long ago'. I render 'from of old' in the literal layer and 'from the beginning of time' only in the dramatic layer, because 'olam' means a very long, unmeasured time rather than a stated starting point.

The Hebrew has 'sins of my youth and my transgressions' with a single noun 'my youth' modifying 'sins' only on the face of it. Whether 'youth' also qualifies 'transgressions' is open; KJV, ASV and Webster all read 'my transgressions' as separate, and I did the same. The Radak/Meiri distinction between chata'ot (unwitting) and pesha' (rebellious) is cited from them and not asserted as a fixed rule of the words.
The last words of the verse are 'for the sake of your goodness'. BBE has 'righteousness', which is wrong for tuv. I kept 'goodness'.
BBE's 'poor in spirit' reflects the overlap of anav with ani, 'poor'. I chose 'humble' for both occurrences, as the KJV's 'meek' is a weaker word in modern English.

notes.note: The poem is an alphabetic acrostic, but a loose one. The verses open aleph (v1, v2), gimel (v3), dalet (v4), he (v5), zayin (v6), chet (v7), tet (v8), yod (v9), kaf (v10), lamed (v11), mem (v12). Bet is carried by בְּךָ, the second word of v2, and vav by וְלַמְּדֵנִי, mid-verse in v5. I mention this in v2 and v5 only, from my own reading of the Hebrew; Radak and Meiri discuss the same gaps, and I cite them for that.
